raw_case_text:
A 39-year-old woman was referred to our department for headache and fever. On admission, brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed no abnormalities with white matter lesions or acute demyelinating lesions. The routine laboratory tests including a complete blood count, liver and renal function, and myocardial enzymes were almost normal. HIV and hepatitis C were negative in the patient. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examinations revealed increased intracranial pressure of 250 mmH2O (normal 80-180 mmH2O), an increased protein level of 510 mg/L (normal 150-450 mg/L), an elevated white cell count of 70 /mul (normal 0-10/mul), and a low glucose level of 2.38 mmol/L (normal 2.8-4.4 mmol/L). The ink stain of CSF was positive; cryptococcal polysaccharide capsular antigen in the CSF was positive; and CSF culture was also positive to cryptococcus neoformans. Collectively, the final diagnosis was cryptococcal meningitis. The weight of the patient was 40 kilograms. Consequently, the patient was treated with L-AMB (10-30 mg/d, gradually increasing in the induction phase), 5-flucytosine (25 mg/kg, 6-hourly), and fluconazole (400-800 mg/d) according to the guideline in China. Dexamethasone (1-5 mg/d) was also used to alleviate inflammation-induced edema intermittently (Figure 1). After 34 days of anti-fungal therapy, the headache and fever of the patient rapidly improved. In addition, CSF culture was negative for Cryptococcus, and she was discharged home after a 48-day course of anti-fungal therapy. Then, she was switched to consolidation therapeutic schedule shifting from L-AMB to fluconazole (400 mg orally, BID) and 5-flucytosine (25 mg/kg 6-hourly) (Figure 1).
L-AMB was discontinued after the patient was discharged home. However, 30 days after discharge, or on the 78th day after the initial anti-fungal therapy with a cumulative dose of 1,115 mg L-AMB therapy course, she suddenly presented with recurrent seizure attacks without any prodromal symptoms. She suffered an abrupt onset of upper extremities twitching; the episodes last for about 1 min without loss of consciousness and then complete recovery. On the second day, she showed hallucinations, altered moods, disorganized speech, aggressive behaviors, and other psychiatric behaviors. Subsequently, she developed a decreased level of consciousness from confusion to lethargy and to coma. On the third day, the patient began to recover following dehydration, rehydration, and sedation treatment, she gradually became awake with return of consciousness. On the fourth day, the central nervous system symptoms completely disappeared, and the patient recovered completely. During this episode, physical examination revealed disorders of consciousness, but pupillary light reflex, Babinski sign, and signs of meningeal irritation were negative. After the episode, she was conscious, and the other clinical neurologic examinations were normal. In addition, after 1 and 3 months of discharged follow-up, the patient was symptom free without any recurrence.
The routine examinations including complete blood count, liver and renal function, lactate dehydrogenase, creatine kinase, myocardial enzymes, and thyroid function tests were negative. Lumbar puncture was performed to exclude the recurrence of cryptococcal meningitis. However, the cryptococcal polysaccharide capsular antigen, ink stain, and culture of CSF did not support cryptococcal meningitis. The examinations of blood and CSF related to autoimmune encephalitis, demyelination, and metabolic diseases were negative.
Cerebral MRI showed bilaterally symmetric hyperintensity on DWI signal and abnormal hyperintensity on T2 weight image in the deep white matter and corpus callosum (Figure 2). The abnormal signals gradually reduced and disappeared 4 days later. A month after the encephalopathy, her brain MRI was almost normal (Figure 2). The electroencephalogram (EEG) was normal during the episode.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 39-year-old woman treated with liposomal amphotericin B, flucytosine, and fluconazole for cryptococcal meningitis presented 30 days after hospital discharge (day 78 of antifungal therapy) with sudden-onset recurrent upper extremity focal motor seizures, visual/auditory hallucinations, aggressive behavior, and progression to coma.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient initially presented with headache and fever and was diagnosed with Cryptococcus neoformans meningitis (ICP 250 mmH2O, positive CSF India ink, CrAg, and culture), receiving 48 days of inpatient antifungal therapy (cumulative liposomal amphotericin B dose 1,115 mg at 10-30 mg/day, 5-flucytosine 25 mg/kg every 6 hours, fluconazole 400-800 mg/day, and intermittent dexamethasone 1-5 mg/day) with CSF sterilization at day 34 and discharge on oral fluconazole (400 mg twice daily) and 5-flucytosine. Thirty days post-discharge (day 78 after treatment initiation), she abruptly developed 1-minute episodes of bilateral upper extremity twitching without loss of consciousness, followed on day 2 by hallucinations, disorganized speech, aggression, lethargy, and coma.
subjective.past_medical_history: Cryptococcus neoformans meningitis diagnosed 78 days prior (sterilized after 34 days of induction therapy); weight 40 kg; HIV- and HCV-negative.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for initial headache and fever, and day 78 abrupt upper limb twitching seizures, hallucinations, mood changes, disorganized speech, aggressive behavior, and coma. Home medications at day 78: oral fluconazole 400 mg twice daily and oral 5-flucytosine 25 mg/kg every 6 hours (following 1,115 mg cumulative L-AmB).

objective.physical_examination: Weight 40 kg; during the day 78-81 acute encephalopathy episode, progressed from confusion to lethargy and coma with preserved pupillary light reflexes and negative Babinski and meningeal irritation signs, recovering full consciousness and normal neurological exam by day 4 of the episode.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine CBC, hepatic and renal function, LDH, creatine kinase, myocardial enzymes, thyroid function, and HIV and HCV serologies were normal or negative during both admissions.
objective.advanced_workup: Initial admission: brain MRI was normal; LP showed ICP 250 mmH2O (normal: 80-180), protein 510 mg/L (normal: 150-450), WBC 70/uL (normal: 0-10), glucose 2.38 mmol/L (normal: 2.8-4.4), and positive CSF India ink, CrAg, and C. neoformans culture. Day 78 encephalopathy admission: repeat LP was negative for CSF CrAg, India ink, and fungal culture, and blood/CSF autoimmune encephalitis, demyelination, and metabolic panels as well as EEG were negative/normal; brain MRI demonstrated bilaterally symmetric T2 and diffusion-weighted (DWI) hyperintensities in the deep white matter and corpus callosum that began resolving within 4 days and normalized at 1 month.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis of reversible antifungal-induced leukoencephalopathy (attributed to delayed liposomal amphotericin B / 5-flucytosine neurotoxicity involving the corpus callosum and bilateral deep white matter) following successful eradication of Cryptococcus neoformans meningitis, confirmed by symmetric reversible DWI/T2 callosal and deep white matter hyperintensities on brain MRI and exclusion of cryptococcal relapse (negative CSF CrAg, India ink, and culture) and autoimmune/metabolic encephalopathy. Managed with withdrawal of offending agents and supportive dehydration, rehydration, and sedation therapy, resulting in complete neurological recovery within 4 days, MRI normalization at 1 month, and sustained remission at 1- and 3-month follow-ups.
